name: ज्ञानकर्मसंन्यासयोग
meaning: The Yoga of Knowledge and Action
teaching: Action done as offering stops binding the doer — it burns in the fire of knowledge like fuel. Krishna widens the lens: this teaching is ancient, the teacher returns age after age, and every sincere path of sacrifice ends in the same seeing. Knowledge is the rarest fire, and everything offered into it is purified. Knowledge here is not information but fire — it burns the bonds of past action and reveals stillness inside motion. The descent of the divine and the lineage of teachers exist to keep that fire findable.
questions: What, in your daily work, could you genuinely treat as an offering rather than a transaction?
Krishna says the wise see 'action in inaction, and inaction in action.' Sit with one day of your life through that lens.
What doubt, left uncut, is quietly governing your decisions?

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
इमं विवस्वते योगं प्रोक्तवानहमव्ययम् ।
विवस्वान्मनवे प्राह मनुरिक्ष्वाकवेऽब्रवीत्॥
verses.transliteration:
imaṃ vivasvate yogaṃ proktavānahamavyayam
vivasvānmanave prāha manurikṣvākave'bravīt
verses.essence: I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvan; Vivasvan told it to Manu; Manu to Ikshvaku.
verses.translation: I taught this imperishable Yoga to Vivasvan; he told it to Manu; Manu proclaimed it to Ikshvaku.

anvaya.form: past active participle, masculine nominative singular (having taught)
adjective, masculine, accusative singular (agrees with yoga)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + व्यय (decay): that which does not decay

verses.explanation: Krishna suddenly gives the teaching a genealogy older than history: sun, first man, first king. The claim is double — this yoga is not an improvisation for Arjuna's crisis but the original operating manual of civilization; and it travels by paramparā, person to person, like fire passed torch to torch.
verses.connection: Opens a new movement: the teaching of chapters 2–3 is now given its lineage and its license.
verses.reflection: Remember that what you are learning is ancient — let the lineage steady your private practice.
verses.background: Chapter 4 opens with Krishna still speaking and no new question from Arjuna. Śrīdhara explains that before expanding the paths of action and knowledge taught in the last two chapters, Krishna first praises them by their lineage. Vivasvān is the sun, Manu his son, and Ikṣvāku the first king of the solar line.
verses.hook: How old is the teaching Krishna is giving, and who received it first?

views.text: The yoga is called imperishable because its fruit, liberation grounded in steadfast knowledge, never decays. It was first given to the Sun so that rulers would have the strength to protect the world.
This is not a teaching invented now to spur Arjuna into battle; the Lord gave it to Vivasvan at the start of the age as the means of release for all beings.
Krishna first praises the teaching by its unbroken descent, preparing both to unfold the paths of action and knowledge further and to disclose his own appearing and vanishing.

The teaching is not new or improvised for the battle; it is eternal and was handed down from a perfect source through teacher and disciple. Such received knowledge is easier and surer than knowledge built up by speculation.

verses.devanagari:
एवं परम्पराप्राप्तमिमं राजर्षयो विदुः ।
स कालेनेह महता योगो नष्टः परन्तप॥
verses.transliteration:
evaṃ paramparāprāptamimaṃ rājarṣayo viduḥ
sa kāleneha mahatā yogo naṣṭaḥ parantapa
verses.essence: Thus received in succession, the royal sages knew it. Through long lapse of time, Parantapa, this yoga was lost to the world.
verses.translation: This, handed down thus in regular succession, the royal sages knew. This Yoga, by long lapse of time, has been lost here, O Parantapa (burner of the foes).

anvaya.parts: परम्परा (succession) + प्राप्त (received): received by an unbroken line
राजन् (king) + ऋषि (sage): kings who are also sages

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine nominative singular (lost)

anvaya.parts: पर (enemy) + तप (scorching): one who scorches enemies

verses.explanation: Two details carry the weight: the keepers were rāja-ṛṣis, king-sages — rulers in the thick of action, not forest recluses; this yoga was always meant for people with kingdoms and battles. And even so, time ate it: truths are not lost by refutation but by generations of half-hearted transmission.
verses.connection: Explains why a restatement (4.3) is needed at all: the torch of 4.1 had gone out.
verses.reflection: Ask what great teaching has decayed in your keeping, and restore one small rite of it.
verses.background: The lineage of 4.1 has reached Ikṣvāku, the first king. This verse carries it on through the royal sages, men who were both kings and sages, and then brings the story to the present, which Śrīdhara reads as the reason people today do not know this yoga.
verses.hook: How was this teaching passed down, and why was it lost?

refs.note: Says God revealed sacred knowledge in the heart of Brahmā, the first-born, at creation, showing that the line of teaching begins with God himself.

views.text: The line snapped because the yoga reached people who were weak and had no control of their senses. Parantapa is one who scorches enemies, like the sun, with the heat of his prowess.
Long lapse of time and the dull understanding of those who heard it caused the loss, and the yoga is described as almost lost rather than wholly gone.
Divine knowledge flows from God through a line of teachers, but over time insincere students distort it. Then God restores it, either by descending himself or through a God-realised saint.

verses.devanagari:
स एवायं मया तेऽद्य योगः प्रोक्तः पुरातनः ।
भक्तोऽसि मे सखा चेति रहस्यं ह्येतदुत्तमम्॥
verses.transliteration:
sa evāyaṃ mayā te'dya yogaḥ proktaḥ purātanaḥ
bhakto'si me sakhā ceti rahasyaṃ hyetaduttamam
verses.essence: That same ancient yoga I have today declared to you, for you are my devotee and friend — this is the supreme secret.
verses.translation: That same ancient Yoga has been today taught to thee by Me, for thou art My devotee and My friend; it is the supreme secret.

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine nominative singular (taught)

anvaya.base: भक्त · devoted one (from √भज्, to love, serve)

verses.explanation: The qualifications for the highest secret are not learning or austerity but two relationships: bhakta and sakhā, devotee and friend. Trust opens what intellect alone cannot — a secret is by definition something given, and giving requires a bond. Arjuna receives the lost yoga not because he is the best philosopher on the field, but because he is the one who loves and is loved.
verses.connection: Completes 4.1–2: the broken lineage is re-lit, and devotion and friendship are named as the bond that carries it.
verses.reflection: Notice that the deepest things are entrusted to friendship — be the kind of friend secrets choose.
verses.background: Having traced the yoga from the sun down to the royal sages and told of its loss, Krishna brings it to the present moment and to Arjuna. Śaṅkara sets the scene: the teaching had passed to people of weak self-control, and the world had turned to aims that do not lead to freedom.
verses.hook: Why does Krishna choose Arjuna to receive this secret teaching?

views.text: What is handed over here is the yoga understood as Knowledge, a profound secret given because Arjuna is devotee and friend.
The yoga is taught in full with all its accessories; being the most hidden knowledge of the Vedanta, it can be known and taught by none but the Lord himself.
The word 'too' marks friendship as secondary: Arjuna's real qualification is devotion, having nothing but the Lord as his goal.
The tradition had been broken, so the Lord tells it again, and he says he would not tell it to anyone else.
The teaching is secret not from selfishness but because it needs a qualification: devotion. Scholarship alone cannot grasp it; Arjuna qualifies because he loves Krishna as a friend.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
अपरं भवतो जन्म परं जन्म विवस्वतः ।
कथमेतद्विजानीयां त्वमादौ प्रोक्तवानिति॥
verses.transliteration:
aparaṃ bhavato janma paraṃ janma vivasvataḥ
kathametadvijānīyāṃ tvamādau proktavāniti
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: your birth was later, Vivasvan's earlier — how am I to understand that you taught it in the beginning?
verses.translation: Later on was Thy birth, and prior to it was the birth of Vivasvan (the Sun); how am I to understand that Thou taughtest this Yoga in the beginning?

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, nominative singular (agrees with birth)
adjective, neuter, nominative singular (agrees with birth)
verb, optative, 1st person singular (how should I)
past active participle, masculine nominative singular (having taught)

verses.explanation: Arjuna does the arithmetic out loud: the sun is older than the man beside him in the chariot. The question is asked half in earnest, half as an opening — he suspects the answer will be larger than chronology, and he wants to hear Krishna say it. Good students build doorways with their doubts.
verses.connection: The natural objection to 4.1 — and the invitation Krishna needs to reveal who is actually speaking.
verses.reflection: Let yourself ask the naive question today; Arjuna's bluntness is why we have this book.
verses.background: Arjuna speaks for the first time in this chapter. Krishna has just claimed to have taught this yoga to the sun at the beginning, yet he stands beside Arjuna as a man of Arjuna's own generation. Śaṅkara says the question is raised so that no one thinks the Lord has contradicted himself.
verses.hook: How could Krishna have taught someone who lived long before him?

views.text: The question serves to remove the doubt of the foolish who deny that Vasudeva is God and all-knowing.
Arjuna already knows Krishna as the Lord; he asks as if he did not, to learn whether the divine birth is real or illusory, and what its manner, body and cause are.
Arjuna's puzzlement about timing opens the way for Krishna to explain how God descends into the world, which the following verses take up.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
बहूनि मे व्यतीतानि जन्मानि तव चार्जुन ।
तान्यहं वेद सर्वाणि न त्वं वेत्थ परन्तप॥
verses.transliteration:
bahūni me vyatītāni janmāni tava cārjuna
tānyahaṃ veda sarvāṇi na tvaṃ vettha parantapa
verses.essence: Many births of mine have passed, and of yours, Arjuna. I know them all; you do not, Parantapa.
verses.translation: Many births of Mine have passed as well as of thine, O Arjuna; I know them all but thou knowest not, O Parantapa (scorcher of foes).

anvaya.form: past participle, neuter nominative plural (have passed)
verb, perfect form with present meaning, 1st person singular (I know)
verb, perfect form with present meaning, 2nd person singular (you know)

anvaya.parts: पर (enemy) + तप (scorching): one who scorches enemies

verses.explanation: The answer begins with a leveling and a difference: both of them have worn many lives — rebirth is the shared condition — but only one of them remembers. The forgetting is the human predicament; the unbroken memory is the divine one. Krishna does not claim a different history from Arjuna's; he claims an unlost one.
verses.connection: Resolves 4.4's chronology: the body beside Arjuna is recent; the speaker is not.
verses.reflection: You too have passed through many selves you no longer remember — bow once to the forgotten ones.
verses.background: Krishna replies to Arjuna's puzzle: how could a man born so recently have taught the ancient sun? Śaṅkara says the reply also targets a deeper doubt that the question stands for, the doubt of the foolish that Krishna is neither God nor all-knowing.
verses.hook: What does Krishna know about past lives that Arjuna does not?

views.text: Arjuna's power of knowing is blocked by merit and demerit; the Lord's is unobstructed because he is by nature eternal, pure, enlightened and free.
The first clause establishes that the Lord's births are real; Arjuna's births are mentioned only as an illustration.

Though God appears in human form, he is not an ordinary being; he keeps his divine powers and full knowledge in every descent, while the soul's knowledge stays limited. Krishna urges Arjuna to cut this doubt with knowledge.

verses.devanagari:
अजोऽपि सन्नव्ययात्मा भूतानामीश्वरोऽपि सन् ।
प्रकृतिं स्वामधिष्ठाय सम्भवाम्यात्ममायया॥
verses.transliteration:
ajo'pi sannavyayātmā bhūtānāmīśvaro'pi san
prakṛtiṃ svāmadhiṣṭhāya sambhavāmyātmamāyayā
verses.essence: Though unborn and imperishable, though Lord of all beings, ruling my own nature I come into being by my own maya.
verses.translation: Though I am unborn, of imperishable nature, and though I am the Lord of all beings, yet, governing My own Nature, I am born by My own Maya.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + ज (born): one who is not born
अव्यय (imperishable) + आत्मन् (self, nature): one whose nature is imperishable

anvaya.base: सम् + √भू · to come into being, be born

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: आत्मन् (own self) + माया (power): by one's own power

verses.explanation: The paradox is stated, not softened: unborn, yet born. The resolution lies in two phrases — adhiṣṭhāya, *having taken charge of* his nature rather than being governed by it, and ātma-māyayā, by his own creative power rather than karma's compulsion. Ordinary birth is being thrown; this is stepping in. Same doorway, opposite direction of force.
verses.connection: Answers how 4.5's rememberer can have births at all: divine birth is sovereign, not sentenced.
verses.reflection: The highest power arrives by choosing limits; honor one limitation of yours as a possible doorway.
verses.background: Krishna has just said that many of his births have passed. That raises the objection Śrīdhara spells out: how can one who has no beginning, cannot perish and is untouched by good and bad deeds be born at all, as other beings are? This verse answers it.
verses.hook: How can one who is unborn and eternal still take birth?

refs.note: States that Brahman has two forms, with form and formless, supporting the claim that God can be both personal and formless.
Explains that scriptures calling God without qualities mean his form is free of material defects, not that he has no form.

views.text: Controlling Vishnu's maya of the three gunas, he appears embodied, as though born; he is not born in reality like an ordinary man.
Maya here means knowledge, that is, will. Without giving up any divine quality, he takes a form of his own choosing; his birth is by will, not forced by karma.
His 'own nature' is pure sattva: taking it up, he descends by his own wish in a form of pure, mighty sattva, with knowledge and power never lost.
The all-powerful God has both a formless aspect and a personal form. His form is not made of matter like ours but by his own divine power, so it is free of material defects.

verses.devanagari:
यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत ।
अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānirbhavati bhārata
abhyutthānamadharmasya tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmyaham
verses.essence: Whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, Bharata, then I send myself forth.
verses.translation: Whenever there is decline of righteousness, O Arjuna, and rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + धर्म (dharma): what is against dharma

verses.explanation: The trigger condition for descent: glāni — dharma not destroyed but wilting, drooping like an unwatered plant — while its opposite stands up. Yadā yadā, 'whenever', makes the clause iterative: divine intervention as a standing law, not a one-time rescue. The verse implies a moral physics of history: the world's balance is watched, and past a threshold the Unborn enters time. Read inwardly too, the promise holds wherever dharma wilts — in an age or in a single life.
verses.connection: Generalizes 4.5–6: the principle behind every divine birth, including the one seated in Arjuna's chariot.
verses.reflection: Watch for the dharma-decline in your own week — and for the help that rises exactly then.
verses.background: Having explained how he takes birth, Krishna turns to when. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as the answer to the natural next question, 'When do you come?'; the verse after it gives the why.
verses.hook: When does God come into the world?

refs.note: God says his births, deeds and names are countless, beyond even his own counting, so his descents are innumerable.
Declares that all of God's descents are complete and perfect, so none should be ranked above another.

views.text: Dharma means the duties of class and stage of life, the means to prosperity and liberation; when they decline he manifests himself through Maya.
No time is fixed for his birth: whenever Vedic dharma declines and its opposite grows, he incarnates by his own will in the manner already stated.
Dharma is what sustains and lifts a person toward liberation; adharma is whatever drags one down into worldliness and ignorance.
When righteousness declines, God descends as an avatar to restore it. His descents are countless and all complete, though in each he displays only the powers his purpose needs.

verses.devanagari:
परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् ।
धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे॥
verses.transliteration:
paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṃ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām
dharmasaṃsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge
verses.essence: For the protection of the good, the destruction of evil-doers, and the establishment of dharma, I come into being age after age.
verses.translation: For the protection of the good, for the destruction of the wicked and for the establishment of righteousness, I am born in every age.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, dative singular (for the purpose of)
noun, masculine, dative singular (for the purpose of)

anvaya.parts: दुस् (bad) + कृत् (doer): one who does wrong

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, dative singular (for the purpose of)
anvaya.parts: धर्म (dharma) + संस्थापन (firm establishing) + अर्थ (purpose): for the purpose of establishing dharma

anvaya.base: सम् + √भू · to come into being, be born

verses.explanation: The mission statement, in three clauses of widening scope: shelter the good, end the destroyers, and — the real objective — dharma-saṃsthāpana, re-founding dharma itself, since rescue without restoration only resets the clock. Yuge yuge promises recurrence: no age is abandoned; the promise keeps its rhythm, again and again. For Arjuna the implication is immediate and unspoken: this war is one such operation, and he is standing inside it.
verses.connection: Specifies the purpose of 4.7's descents — and silently reframes Kurukshetra as one of them.
verses.reflection: Protect one good thing today, discourage one corrosion, and you participate in the avatara's work.
verses.background: Krishna has said when he takes birth; the remaining question, 'For what purpose?', is answered here. Śrīdhara introduces the verse with exactly that question, and with it Krishna completes the account of his descent begun at 4.5.
verses.hook: Why does God take birth in the world, age after age?

refs.note: Says Rāma freed only one Ahalyā in person, but his name has since reformed countless souls, showing how a descent nourishes devotion.

views.text: The Lord manifests himself in every age to protect the pious who follow the virtuous path, to destroy sinful evil-doers, and to establish virtue fully.
The chief purpose is to let devotees, who cannot bear separation, see his form and deeds and speak with him; destroying the wicked is secondary, and no age is excluded.
Punishing the wicked is not cruelty: as a mother who both fondles and scolds a child is not unkind, so the Lord rules over both virtue and fault.
The good are the selfless who serve others and give themselves to contemplation; the wicked are the greedy, violent and dishonest who take what belongs to others.
God could protect, destroy and teach without descending, so the deeper purpose is to give souls his names, forms and pastimes as an easy basis for devotion, which is the highest dharma.

verses.devanagari:
जन्म कर्म च मे दिव्यमेवं यो वेत्ति तत्त्वतः ।
त्यक्त्वा देहं पुनर्जन्म नैति मामेति सोऽर्जुन॥
verses.transliteration:
janma karma ca me divyamevaṃ yo vetti tattvataḥ
tyaktvā dehaṃ punarjanma naiti māmeti so'rjuna
verses.essence: One who truly knows my divine birth and action, on leaving the body is not born again — that one comes to me.
verses.translation: He who thus know, in their true light, My divine birth and action, having abandoned the body, is not born again, he comes to Me, O Arjuna.

anvaya.form: pronoun, accusative singular (to me, as goal)

verses.explanation: An astonishing exchange rate: correct understanding of one fact — that this birth and these acts are divyam, divine and unforced — is itself liberating. Why so much from mere knowing? Because to truly see one being act without compulsion is to discover that action without bondage exists, and that discovery unlocks one's own. The knower of the free becomes free.
verses.connection: Attaches the fruit to 4.6–8: the doctrine of descent is not trivia — rightly grasped, it is a door.
verses.reflection: Hold the divine births as real once today, and notice what that does to your sense of company.
verses.background: Krishna has described his birth, unborn yet appearing by his own power, and the purposes of his coming in every age. Śrīdhara presents this verse as the result for the one who understands such a birth as taken by choice and such deeds as done for others' good.
verses.hook: What happens to someone who truly understands Krishna's divine birth and deeds?

refs.note: Describes Krishna appearing at birth before Vasudeva and Devakī in his four-armed form, showing his birth was not ordinary.
Compares Krishna's appearance to the full moon rising in the east, a divine manifestation rather than a normal birth.

views.text: The divine birth is a form of Maya and the divine acts are things like protecting the good; whoever knows them as they really are is liberated.
True knowledge of his birth and deeds destroys the sins that block taking refuge in him; loving him and fixed on him alone, such a person reaches him.
His body is made not by the results of action but by his own freedom and highest yogic knowledge; to know this is to realise it in one's own Self as well.
'Leaving the body' is read as giving up identification with the body; the knower then attains the Lord rather than another birth.
Devotion to God's personal form needs divine feelings toward his birth and deeds. His actions are selfless pastimes, not work, and his birth is not from a womb; faith in this frees one from rebirth.

verses.devanagari:
वीतरागभयक्रोधा मन्मया मामुपाश्रिताः ।
बहवो ज्ञानतपसा पूता मद्भावमागताः॥
verses.transliteration:
vītarāgabhayakrodhā manmayā māmupāśritāḥ
bahavo jñānatapasā pūtā madbhāvamāgatāḥ
verses.essence: Freed from passion, fear and anger, absorbed in me, taking refuge in me, purified by the fire of knowledge, many have attained my being.
verses.translation: Freed from attachment, fear and anger, absorbed in Me, taking refuge in Me, purified by the fire of knowledge, many have attained to My Being.

anvaya.meaning: free from attachment, fear and anger
anvaya.base: वीत · gone; राग · attachment; भय · fear; क्रोध · anger
anvaya.parts: वीत (gone) + राग (attachment) + भय (fear) + क्रोध (anger): those from whom these have gone
मत् (me) + मय (made of, full of): filled with me

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine nominative plural (having taken refuge)

anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + तपस् (austerity): the austerity that is knowledge

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine nominative plural (purified)

anvaya.parts: मत् (me) + भाव (state): my own state

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine nominative plural (have come to)

verses.explanation: Precedent for the promise of 4.9: bahavaḥ, many — this road has traffic history. The sequence is exact: release the three contractions (craving, fear, anger), fill the cleared space with the Divine (man-mayāḥ — made of Me), and let jñāna work as tapas, knowledge itself as the purifying fire. The destination is not proximity but mad-bhāvam: his very mode of being.
verses.connection: Shows 4.9's door already worn smooth by use — and the inner steps of those who walked through.
verses.reflection: Take refuge from one fear today by knowledge of what you are, not by distraction.
verses.background: Krishna has just promised freedom from rebirth to whoever truly knows his divine birth and deeds. Śaṅkara links this verse to that promise: the way is not newly opened, and people of earlier times already walked it.
verses.hook: How have so many people in the past reached God?

refs.note: Says that without the water of loving devotion to Rāma, the inner dirt of the mind never washes away.

views.text: The absorbed are knowers of Brahman who see their identity with God; naming the austerity of Knowledge shows that steadfastness in Knowledge needs no other austerity.
The purifying austerity is the knowledge of the truth of the Lord's birth and deeds just described.
They are free of anger and the rest because every desire is fulfilled in being full of him; they do what must be done, with no fruit for themselves.
Knowing his compassion clears attachment, fear and anger; knowledge with one's own duty as its ripening austerity purifies them, and 'my state' means union with him.

Attachment is the root of fear and anger and dirties the mind. Detaching the mind from the world and absorbing it in God, who is beyond nature's qualities, purifies it, and many have reached God this way.

verses.devanagari:
ये यथा मां प्रपद्यन्ते तांस्तथैव भजाम्यहम् ।
मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः॥
verses.transliteration:
ye yathā māṃ prapadyante tāṃstathaiva bhajāmyaham
mama vartmānuvartante manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ
verses.essence: In whatever way people approach me, in that very way I receive them; in every way, Partha, people follow my path.
verses.translation: In whatever way men approach Me even so do I reward them; My path do men tread in all ways, O Arjuna.

anvaya.base: प्र + √पद् · to go to, resort to

verses.explanation: One of the Gita's widest sentences. The divine response is a mirror: however people come, and whatever they seek, they are met in that same way — the seeker of fruits receives fruits, the seeker of freedom receives freedom, and no one is favoured out of love or aversion. The second line widens further: mama vartma... sarvaśaḥ — in every way, the roads humans walk, knowingly or not, lead along his road. Every sincere approach is answered in its own dialect, and answered by the same One.
verses.connection: Universalizes 4.10's 'many': the historical walkers were on countless roads, and all of them counted.
verses.reflection: However you approach the sacred today, trust that the approach is being answered in kind.
verses.background: Krishna has said that many, purified and taking refuge in him, reached his being. An objection follows, which Śaṅkara voices: does he then favour some and reject others, granting union with himself to a few only? This verse is his reply.
verses.hook: Does God respond to everyone in the same way?

refs.note: Rāma tells Hanumān he would give his life for one service and stay forever indebted for the rest, showing God binds himself to devotees' love.

views.text: He favours each by the fruit they seek: rewards to those after rewards, knowledge to seekers of liberation, liberation to the wise, relief to the suffering — never out of love or aversion.
To those who seek him in whatever form they like, he reveals himself in that very form, even in images, so they experience him with their own senses.
Even those who worship Indra and other gods follow his path, since he is the one served in those forms too; he does not neglect them.
God reciprocates according to how one approaches him: to non-believers as the impartial law of karma, to the surrendered as a caring mother, even making himself indebted to their selfless love.

verses.devanagari:
काङ्क्षन्तः कर्मणां सिद्धिं यजन्त इह देवताः ।
क्षिप्रं हि मानुषे लोके सिद्धिर्भवति कर्मजा॥
verses.transliteration:
kāṅkṣantaḥ karmaṇāṃ siddhiṃ yajanta iha devatāḥ
kṣipraṃ hi mānuṣe loke siddhirbhavati karmajā
verses.essence: Desiring success in their works, people here sacrifice to the gods — for in the human world, success from action comes quickly.
verses.translation: Those who long for success in action in this world sacrifice to the gods; because success is quickly attained by men through action.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine nominative plural (longing for)
adjective, feminine, nominative singular (agrees with success)
anvaya.parts: कर्मन् (action) + ज (born): arising from action

verses.explanation: A sociological aside without contempt: most religion is transactional because transactions pay fast. Rain, victory, children — the deities' department delivers on human timescales, while the path of 4.10 pays in a currency that takes lifetimes to recognize. The verse explains the market; it does not curse the customers.
verses.connection: The realistic counterpoint to 4.11: most approaches are quick-yield ones — and even those are received.
verses.reflection: Notice your preference for fast results — and what slower, truer thing it keeps outbidding.
verses.background: Krishna has said he meets each person in the way they come to him. The next question, as Śrīdhara puts it, is why, in that case, people do not all worship him for liberation alone, and turn instead to other gods.
verses.hook: Why do people seeking worldly success worship the gods?

views.text: Worship of other gods springs from not knowing the Self, which splits worshipper from worshipped; results come quickly in the human world because scriptural eligibility for rites applies there.
People want sons, cattle, food and heaven fast, so they propitiate Indra and others; hardly anyone, weary of samsara, takes up desireless karma yoga, which is truly the Lord's worship.
The success meant here, both enjoyment and liberation, is won in this human world alone and nowhere else.
The celestial gods grant quick but temporary material boons, using power received from the Supreme. The wise skip the intermediary and go straight to the Supreme Lord.

verses.devanagari:
चातुर्वर्ण्यं मया सृष्टं गुणकर्मविभागशः ।
तस्य कर्तारमपि मां विद्ध्यकर्तारमव्ययम्॥
verses.transliteration:
cāturvarṇyaṃ mayā sṛṣṭaṃ guṇakarmavibhāgaśaḥ
tasya kartāramapi māṃ viddhyakartāramavyayam
verses.essence: The fourfold order was created by me according to division of guna and action. Though its maker, know me as the actionless, immutable non-doer.
verses.translation: The fourfold caste has been created by Me according to the differentiation of Guna and Karma; though I am the author thereof know Me as non-doer and immutable.

anvaya.parts: चतुर् (four) + वर्ण (class), with a suffix that keeps the same sense: the four classes as one order

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter nominative singular (created)

anvaya.meaning: by division of qualities and works
anvaya.parts: गुण (quality) + कर्म (work) + विभाग (division) + -शः (according to): according to the division of qualities and works
अ (not) + कर्तृ (doer): one who does not act
अ (not) + व्यय (decay): that which does not change

verses.explanation: Read the basis the verse itself gives: guṇa-karma-vibhāgaśaḥ — by the division of qualities and works. It names temperament and function as the principle of the fourfold order and says nothing here about birth; the classical commentators map each varṇa to its dominant guṇa and its duties. Its deeper cargo is the paradox in the second line: maker, yet non-doer — the order arises through his power while he remains untouched, the template for the unattached action this whole chapter teaches.
verses.connection: Extends 4.6's sovereign action to world-making itself: even ordering society leaves no fingerprint on the Orderer.
verses.reflection: Read your own qualities and works honestly; let them, not labels, tell you your station.
verses.background: Krishna has been answering the charge that he treats people unequally. Śrīdhara presses it further: the world shows higher and lower among its four social orders and their work, and Krishna made that order, so how can he be impartial? This verse takes up that objection.
verses.hook: On what basis are people's four kinds of work divided?

views.text: He is the agent only from the empirical standpoint of maya; from the highest standpoint he is a non-agent and changeless, beyond birth and death.
'Created' stands for creating, protecting and withdrawing the whole universe, from Brahma to a blade of grass; he is its agent yet a non-agent.
The verse answers the charge of partiality: he made the varied order, but as regards its fruits he is the non-doer.

The four occupational classes are based on people's qualities and natures, not birth, and are not fixed. God created the scheme yet is not the doer, like impartial rain that feeds every seed differently.

verses.devanagari:
न मां कर्माणि लिम्पन्ति न मे कर्मफले स्पृहा ।
इति मां योऽभिजानाति कर्मभिर्न स बध्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
na māṃ karmāṇi limpanti na me karmaphale spṛhā
iti māṃ yo'bhijānāti karmabhirna sa badhyate
verses.essence: Actions do not stain me, nor have I craving for their fruit. One who knows me thus is not bound by actions.
verses.translation: Actions do not taint Me, nor have I a desire for the fruit of actions. He who knows Me thus is not bound by actions.

anvaya.form: pronoun, genitive singular (in me / for me)

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + फल (fruit): the fruit of action

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is bound)

verses.explanation: The mechanism of divine immunity, stated so it can be borrowed: actions limpanti — smear, stain — only where craving for the fruit gives them adhesive. No spṛhā, no stickiness. And again the strange grace of 4.9: merely *knowing* this about Krishna transmits the immunity, because what is truly understood begins to be imitated from within.
verses.connection: Explains 4.13's maker-non-doer paradox — and offers the same loophole to whoever comprehends it.
verses.reflection: Work one hour today the way water moves over a lotus leaf — touching everything, stained by nothing.
verses.background: Krishna has just called himself the maker of the fourfold order and yet a non-doer. This verse gives the grounds for that claim, which Śaṅkara says holds from the highest standpoint, though from the everyday view Krishna is the maker.
verses.hook: Why do actions never bind God, and what does knowing this do?

refs.note: Says the powerful are never stained, like the sun, fire and the Ganges, which purify what touches them.
Says devotees and sages are not bound by action, so how could the Lord, who takes form by his own will, be bound.

views.text: Actions do not taint him because he has no egoism; whoever knows him thus as his own Self, and himself as a non-agent without hankering, is likewise not bound.
The differences among gods, men and others come from beings' own karma; the Lord is only the operative cause, and knowing him as agent yet non-agent frees one from old karma.
Like space, he is untouched because he has no desire; whoever contemplates everywhere that nothing exists other than Vasudeva cannot be bound by action.
God acts only from compassion, never for personal gain, so his actions leave no karmic stain. Saints who act wholly in love for him likewise rise above karmic bondage.

verses.devanagari:
एवं ज्ञात्वा कृतं कर्म पूर्वैरपि मुमुक्षुभिः ।
कुरु कर्मैव तस्मात्त्वं पूर्वैः पूर्वतरं कृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
evaṃ jñātvā kṛtaṃ karma pūrvairapi mumukṣubhiḥ
kuru karmaiva tasmāttvaṃ pūrvaiḥ pūrvataraṃ kṛtam
verses.essence: Knowing this, the ancient seekers of liberation also performed action. Therefore do action, as the ancients did of old.
verses.translation: Having known this, the ancient seekers after freedom also performed action; therefore do thou also perform action, as did the ancients in days of yore.

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter nominative singular (done)
adjective used as noun, masculine, instrumental plural (by)

anvaya.base: मुमुक्षु · one who desires liberation (from √मुच्, to free)

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, instrumental plural (by)
past passive participle, neuter nominative singular (done)

verses.explanation: The clinching precedent: mumukṣubhiḥ — those whose one desire was liberation itself — did not quit the field; they worked, armored by the knowledge of 4.14. If the most freedom-hungry people in history chose action, action cannot be freedom's enemy. Tradition here is not a cage but a trail of footprints across difficult ground.
verses.connection: Closes the avatara section's practical loop: what the Lord does (4.13–14), the liberation-seekers copied — now Arjuna's turn.
verses.reflection: The ancients sought freedom and still acted; let their precedent end your either-or today.
verses.background: Śrīdhara marks a turn here: the four verses from 4.11 dealt with a side issue, whether the Lord is partial, and now Krishna returns to the path of action taught earlier in order to develop it. Arjuna has still not agreed to fight.
verses.hook: Why did the seekers of old keep acting after gaining wisdom?

views.text: Do not sit idle or renounce: act for self-purification if you lack Self-knowledge, or to keep people from going astray if you have it, as Janaka and others did.
Having shed sin through this knowledge of the Lord, act as Vivasvan, Manu and the ancients did, in the way he taught them then.
Sages who want nothing material still work, to serve and please God and from compassion for suffering souls, knowing such devoted work cannot bind them. Krishna asks Arjuna to do the same.

verses.devanagari:
किं कर्म किमकर्मेति कवयोऽप्यत्र मोहिताः ।
तत्ते कर्म प्रवक्ष्यामि यज्ज्ञात्वा मोक्ष्यसेऽशुभात्॥
verses.transliteration:
kiṃ karma kimakarmeti kavayo'pyatra mohitāḥ
tatte karma pravakṣyāmi yajjñātvā mokṣyase'śubhāt
verses.essence: What is action? What is inaction? Even the wise are bewildered here. I shall teach you that action, knowing which you will be freed from evil.
verses.translation: What is action? What is inaction? As to this even the wise are confused. Therefore I shall teach thee such action (the nature of action and inaction) by knowing which thou shalt be liberated from the evil (of Samsara, the wheel of birth and death).

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + कर्मन् (action): absence of action

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine nominative plural (bewildered)
verb, future, 2nd person singular (you will be freed)

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + शुभ (auspicious): what is ill

verses.explanation: A humbling admission opens the chapter's deepest passage: kavayo 'pi — even the poets-seers lose their way in this question. Because the answer is not behavioral: doing and not-doing cannot be told apart by watching the hands. Krishna promises a redefinition radical enough that even experts needed it.
verses.connection: Pivot to the chapter's core inquiry (4.16–23): the metaphysics of action that 4.13–15 presupposed.
verses.reflection: Admit that action and inaction puzzle even the wise — then welcome instruction over improvisation.
verses.background: Krishna has told Arjuna to act as the ancients did. Śaṅkara imagines Arjuna asking why the ancients need mentioning if he will act on Krishna's word anyway; the answer is that action is a genuinely hard matter, and this verse opens a new section on it.
verses.hook: Why do even wise people get confused about what right action is?

refs.note: Yama says true dharma is laid down by God himself, and even sages and gods cannot fully know it.

views.text: One should not think action is simply bodily movement and inaction simply sitting still; the matter needs real understanding, which frees one from transmigration.
'Inaction' here means knowledge of the self's true nature; he will teach a form of action that contains that knowledge within it.
This must be worked out together with knowers of truth, not taken from mere popular custom.
Right action cannot be settled by speculation, since duty varies with circumstance and the scriptures can seem to conflict. Only God fully knows dharma, so Krishna now explains it.

verses.devanagari:
कर्मणो ह्यपि बोद्धव्यं बोद्धव्यं च विकर्मणः ।
अकर्मणश्च बोद्धव्यं गहना कर्मणो गतिः॥
verses.transliteration:
karmaṇo hyapi boddhavyaṃ boddhavyaṃ ca vikarmaṇaḥ
akarmaṇaśca boddhavyaṃ gahanā karmaṇo gatiḥ
verses.essence: For the nature of action must be understood, and of wrong action, and of inaction — profound is the way of action.
verses.translation: For verily (the true nature) of action (enjoined by the scriptures) should be known, also (that) of forbidden (or unlawful) action, and of inaction; hard to understand is the nature (path) of action.

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter nominative singular (must be known)
gerundive, neuter nominative singular (must be known)

anvaya.parts: वि (apart, amiss) + कर्मन् (action): action gone astray
अ (not) + कर्मन् (action): absence of action

anvaya.form: gerundive, neuter nominative singular (must be known)
adjective, feminine, nominative singular (agrees with course)

verses.explanation: Three categories, one warning: karma, vikarma (action gone wrong), akarma — and gahanā, the path is a thicket, dense and trackless. The triple repetition of boddhavyam, 'must be understood', hammers that this is knowledge-work, not rule-following. Morality by checklist fails exactly where it matters most.
verses.connection: Justifies 4.16's claim that experts get lost: the terrain itself is gahana, deep forest.
verses.reflection: Distinguish today between right action, wrong action, and the inaction that is also an act.
verses.background: Krishna has promised to explain action and inaction, saying even the wise are confused about them. An objection stands in the way, which Śaṅkara voices: surely everyone knows that action is bodily movement and inaction is sitting still, so what is there to learn?
verses.hook: What three kinds of action must you learn to tell apart?

views.text: Something must be grasped about enjoined action, prohibited action and inaction, meaning sitting quietly; the true nature of all three is hard to know.
Vikarma means the varied forms of rites, obligatory, occasional and desire-prompted; their differing fruits must be set aside, since scripture aims at release alone.
There is harm within enjoined action and good within forbidden action, so no rule settles it; only the fire of wisdom can burn all action, good and bad.

Work falls into three kinds: action recommended by scripture to purify the mind, forbidden action that degrades the soul, and inaction, meaning work done without attachment purely for God, which creates no karmic bondage.

verses.devanagari:
कर्मण्यकर्म यः पश्येदकर्मणि च कर्म यः ।
स बुद्धिमान्मनुष्येषु स युक्तः कृत्स्नकर्मकृत्॥
verses.transliteration:
karmaṇyakarma yaḥ paśyedakarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ
sa buddhimānmanuṣyeṣu sa yuktaḥ kṛtsnakarmakṛt
verses.essence: One who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise among humans — a yogi, a doer of all action.
verses.translation: He who seeth inaction in action and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is a Yogi and performer of all actions.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + कर्मन् (action): absence of action

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine nominative singular (joined in yoga)

anvaya.base: कृत्स्न · whole; कर्मन् · action; कृत् · doer
anvaya.parts: कृत्स्न (all) + कर्म (action) + कृत् (doer): one who has done all action

verses.explanation: The famous double inversion. In action, inaction: the sage in full motion, with doership and craving absent, generates no karmic residue — the engine runs, nothing burns onto the self. In inaction, action: the abstainer of 3.6, body parked, mind seething, accrues karma while doing nothing. The ledger reads intent and identification, never the muscles. This single verse is the answer promised in 4.16: this seeing, not any doing or refraining, is what makes one buddhimān among humans.
verses.connection: The summit of 4.16–17: action and inaction redefined from the inside out.
verses.reflection: Find the stillness inside one busy task today, and the hidden current inside one quiet hour.
verses.background: Having said that the way of action is hard to fathom, Krishna now gives the teaching he promised in 4.16. Śaṅkara introduces it as the statement of what action and inaction really are, the thing that had to be understood.
verses.hook: How can action be a kind of inaction, and inaction be action?

views.text: The ignorant perceive action and inaction contrarily, like water in a mirage or trees seeming to move from a boat; the wise see that the Self never acts.
'Inaction' is knowledge of the self: through contemplation one sees that the work being done is itself a form of knowledge, and that knowledge is held within karma yoga.
In total tranquillity he sees his own acts as no acts; in the fully risen state he recognises the acts of others as his own — so he does all and does nothing.
Work done as worship of the Lord does not bind, so it is 'inaction'; failing to do one's enjoined duty incurs fault, so that non-doing is 'action'.

Dropping duties out of laziness while the mind dwells on pleasures is really sinful action. Doing duties without attachment, offering the fruits to God, is inaction within action, as saintly kings showed.

verses.devanagari:
यस्य सर्वे समारम्भाः कामसङ्कल्पवर्जिताः ।
ज्ञानाग्निदग्धकर्माणं तमाहुः पण्डितं बुधाः॥
verses.transliteration:
yasya sarve samārambhāḥ kāmasaṅkalpavarjitāḥ
jñānāgnidagdhakarmāṇaṃ tamāhuḥ paṇḍitaṃ budhāḥ
verses.essence: One whose every undertaking is free of desire and scheme, whose actions are burned in the fire of knowledge — the wise call that one a sage.
verses.translation: He whose undertakings are all devoid of desires and (selfish) purposes and whose actions have been burnt by the fire of knowledge, him the wise call a sage.

anvaya.meaning: free of desire and its scheming
anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + सङ्कल्प (intention) + वर्जित (devoid of): devoid of desire and the intent behind it

anvaya.meaning: whose actions are burnt by knowledge-fire
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + अग्नि (fire) + दग्ध (burnt) + कर्मन् (action): one whose actions are burnt in the fire of knowledge

anvaya.form: verb, perfect form with present meaning, 3rd person plural (they call)

verses.explanation: The portrait of 4.18's seer begins. Kāma-saṅkalpa is the two-stroke engine of bondage — the want, and the plotting that crystallizes around it; remove both and undertakings continue, oddly lighter. Jñānāgni — knowledge as fire — introduces the chapter's closing image: understanding does not merely inform action, it incinerates its binding residue on contact.
verses.connection: Begins translating 4.18's paradox into a recognizable human being (4.19–23).
verses.reflection: Let one undertaking today be free of desire's blueprint — and feel its karma burning clean.
verses.background: Krishna has just called the person who sees inaction in action wise among people, a yogi. Śaṅkara takes this verse as praise of that way of seeing: it names the marks by which knowers recognise such a person as truly learned.
verses.hook: What kind of person do the wise call truly learned?

views.text: Saṅkalpa is the thought that causes desire; such a person's acts are mere movements, for maintaining the body or guiding others, and seeing inaction in action is the fire that burns them.
Saṅkalpa is the false identification of the self with Prakriti; knowledge of the self, arising alongside one's work, burns up past karma, making him a true karma yogin.
Works done without desire purify the mind, and the knowledge born there burns them, turning action into non-action.

Once the soul realises its bliss lies in loving service to God, not sense objects, it offers every act to him. Such actions produce no karmic reactions; they are burnt in the fire of divine knowledge.

verses.devanagari:
त्यक्त्वा कर्मफलासङ्गं नित्यतृप्तो निराश्रयः ।
कर्मण्यभिप्रवृत्तोऽपि नैव किञ्चित्करोति सः॥
verses.transliteration:
tyaktvā karmaphalāsaṅgaṃ nityatṛpto nirāśrayaḥ
karmaṇyabhipravṛtto'pi naiva kiñcitkaroti saḥ
verses.essence: Abandoning attachment to the fruit of action, ever content, dependent on nothing — though engaged in action, such a one does nothing at all.
verses.translation: Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of the action, ever content, depending on nothing, he does not do anything though engaged in activity.

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + फल (fruit) + आसङ्ग (attachment): attachment to the fruit of action
नित्य (always) + तृप्त (satisfied): always satisfied
निर् (without) + आश्रय (support): one who leans on nothing

verses.explanation: The paradox stated at maximum voltage: abhipravṛttaḥ — plunged into activity — and yet 'does nothing at all.' The supports are two freedoms: nitya-tṛpta, contentment not awaiting the outcome, and nirāśraya, leaning on nothing external for standing. Doing without a doer hungry inside it is, karmically, a kind of perfect stillness in motion.
verses.connection: Restates 4.18's 'inaction in action' as lived posture: full throttle, zero grip.
verses.reflection: Begin something today without leaning on its outcome — content, independent, fully engaged.
verses.background: Krishna continues describing the sage whose works are burned in the fire of knowledge. Here he takes the case Śaṅkara spells out: a person of such knowledge who, for whatever reason, cannot give up action and stays at work as before, partly to keep others from going astray.
verses.hook: How can someone be fully active and yet do nothing at all?

views.text: If such a knower stays in action to keep people from going astray or to avoid the censure of the wise, he still does nothing, because he has realised the actionless Self.
Ever content means satisfied with the eternal self; depending on nothing means not leaning on transient Prakriti. Such action is the practice of knowledge in the form of work.
Content in his own bliss, he needs no support for gaining or keeping things, so even his engaged action becomes non-action.
Like a man who has the king's favour and needs no minister or official, one who has realised the Self depends on nothing.
Whether something counts as action depends on the mind, not outer appearance. Those absorbed in God and depending on nothing else remain non-doers inwardly, whatever they do outwardly.

verses.devanagari:
निराशीर्यतचित्तात्मा त्यक्तसर्वपरिग्रहः ।
शारीरं केवलं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम्॥
verses.transliteration:
nirāśīryatacittātmā tyaktasarvaparigrahaḥ
śārīraṃ kevalaṃ karma kurvannāpnoti kilbiṣam
verses.essence: Without longing, mind and self restrained, all possessions surrendered, performing action with the body alone — one incurs no fault.
verses.translation: Without hope and with the mind and the self controlled, having abandoned all covetousness, doing mere bodily action, he incurs no sin.

anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: निर् (without) + आशिस् (wish, hope): one from whom wishes have gone

anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: यत (controlled) + चित्त (mind) + आत्मन् (self, body): one by whom mind and body are controlled

anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: त्यक्त (abandoned) + सर्व (all) + परिग्रह (possession, ownership): one by whom all possessions are abandoned

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, accusative singular, agreeing with कर्म
adjective, neuter, accusative singular, agreeing with कर्म
present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while doing)

verses.explanation: The minimal case: action pared down to śārīraṁ kevalam — what the body must do to live and serve — with the three great accumulators (hope, mental sprawl, ownership) shut off. Such action passes through the person like light through glass. This is the floor of blameless living; the ceiling was 4.20's full engagement.
verses.connection: Gives 4.20 its ascetic register: even at survival-level action, the same principle holds.
verses.reflection: Do one bodily task today with hope and ownership both set down — and notice no residue forms.
verses.background: The description turns from the sage who keeps working to the one who has given up all undertakings. Śaṅkara reads this verse as being about the renunciant monk, who no longer acts for any result, seen or unseen, and makes effort only to keep the body alive.
verses.hook: Can you act in the world without incurring sin?

views.text: Kilbiṣa here covers merit as well as sin, since for a seeker of liberation even righteousness binds. 'Bodily action' means only what keeps the body alive, done without any sense of being the doer.
Describes a karma-yogin whose goal is the self, so he claims nothing in matter as his own. Such work alone brings the vision of the self; no separate practice of jñāna-yoga is needed.

Two stages are read here: the striver doing work merely with the body, free of the conceit of agency, is not bound; the one established in yoga, doing only what sustains the body, such as begging food, incurs no fault for leaving rites undone.
As worldly law weighs intention over the act itself, those who act with no attachment or sense of ownership, only to please God, incur no sin.

verses.devanagari:
यदृच्छालाभसन्तुष्टो द्वन्द्वातीतो विमत्सरः ।
समः सिद्धावसिद्धौ च कृत्वापि न निबध्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yadṛcchālābhasantuṣṭo dvandvātīto vimatsaraḥ
samaḥ siddhāvasiddhau ca kṛtvāpi na nibadhyate
verses.essence: Content with whatever comes unsought, beyond the pairs, free of envy, equal in success and failure — even acting, one is not bound.
verses.translation: Content with what comes to him without effort, free from the pairs of opposites and envy, even-minded in success and failure, though acting, he is not bound.

anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: यदृच्छा (chance, the unsought) + लाभ (gain) + सन्तुष्ट (content): content with gain that comes by chance

anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: द्वन्द्व (pair of opposites) + अतीत (gone beyond): one who has gone past heat and cold and the like

anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: वि (without) + मत्सर (envy, spite): one without envy
अ (not) + सिद्धि (success): non-success

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is bound)

verses.explanation: Four signatures of the unbound worker, each a closed leak: takes what the day brings (yadṛcchā-lābha) instead of campaigning for more; stands outside the hot-cold, praise-blame seesaw; vimatsara — does not measure himself against others' plates; and meets siddhi and asiddhi with the same face. Where nothing is leaking, nothing binds.
verses.connection: Completes the portrait of 4.19–21 with its social and emotional weather — equanimity as the seal.
verses.reflection: Be satisfied with what arrives unsought today, just once, and taste the rare flavor of enough.
verses.background: The previous verse left the renunciant doing only what keeps the body going. That raises the question of how he gets even his food, and Śaṅkara links this verse to the rule for alms: take what comes unasked and unplanned.
verses.hook: How can you stay unbound while facing success and failure?

views.text: Pictures a monk going for alms: people call him an agent, but from his own realization he does nothing, because action and its cause have been burnt in the fire of knowledge.
'Free from ill-will' means bearing no grudge toward others, seeing one's own past karma as the cause of one's hardships. Such a karma-yogin escapes saṃsāra without a separate jñāna-yoga.
Reads nibadhyate closely: the Self binds itself by taking on the stain of desire for fruits. Insentient action has no power of its own to bind anyone.
Life's dualities cannot be avoided. We rise above them by detaching from the fruits, doing our duty for God and accepting both good and bad outcomes as his will.

verses.devanagari:
गतसङ्गस्य मुक्तस्य ज्ञानावस्थितचेतसः ।
यज्ञायाचरतः कर्म समग्रं प्रविलीयते॥
verses.transliteration:
gatasaṅgasya muktasya jñānāvasthitacetasaḥ
yajñāyācarataḥ karma samagraṃ pravilīyate
verses.essence: For one unattached and free, mind established in knowledge, acting for sacrifice — all karma dissolves entirely.
verses.translation: To one who is devoid of attachment, who is liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, who works for the sake of sacrifice (for the sake of God), the whole action is dissolved.

anvaya.meaning: of one whose attachment is gone
anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, genitive singular (of him)
anvaya.parts: गत (gone) + सङ्ग (attachment): one whose attachment has gone

anvaya.form: past participle used as a noun, masculine, genitive singular (of him)

anvaya.meaning: whose mind is fixed in knowledge
anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, genitive singular (of him)
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + अवस्थित (established) + चेतस् (mind): one whose mind is established in knowledge

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, dative singular (for the sake of)
present participle, masculine, genitive singular (of one doing)
adjective, neuter, nominative singular, agreeing with कर्म
verb, present, middle voice, 3rd person singular

verses.explanation: The section's closing chord gathers its three notes: attachment gone, mind seated in knowledge, and the act offered as yajña — chapter 3's word returning, about to be vastly enlarged. Pravilīyate: the karma does not get balanced or repaid; it melts, like writing in water. Action can be made completely traceless.
verses.connection: Seals 4.18–22 and hands the torch to the yajna-expansion of 4.24–33.
verses.reflection: Work today as worship and watch the action dissolve like the offering it has become.
verses.background: This is the last of the verses about the person whose actions no longer bind, the one Śaṅkara says has been shown, in 4.20, to do nothing even while acting. Krishna now speaks of where that person's remaining work goes.
verses.hook: What happens to the karma of one who works as an offering?

refs.note: States that the soul is by nature God's eternal servant, the understanding from which offering every action to him follows.

views.text: Samagram is taken as 'together with its result': the action of the freed one is destroyed whole, consequence and all, without bearing fruit.

What dissolves is the beginningless load of karma that causes bondage. The commentary marks a turn here: from contemplating the self as distinct from matter to contemplating the Supreme Person as one's own soul.

Yajñāya means 'for the Supreme Lord'; the whole of karma, with its latent impressions, becomes non-action. For one already established in yoga it means acting to protect sacrifice and hold the world together.
Dedicating all actions to God flows from knowing that the soul is his eternal servant. Those established in this understanding are released from the reactions of their work.

verses.devanagari:
ब्रह्मार्पणं ब्रह्म हविर्ब्रह्माग्नौ ब्रह्मणा हुतम् ।
ब्रह्मैव तेन गन्तव्यं ब्रह्मकर्मसमाधिना॥
verses.transliteration:
brahmārpaṇaṃ brahma havirbrahmāgnau brahmaṇā hutam
brahmaiva tena gantavyaṃ brahmakarmasamādhinā
verses.essence: Brahman is the offering, Brahman the oblation, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman; Brahman is reached by one who sees Brahman in every act.
verses.translation: Brahman is the oblation; Brahman is the melted butter (ghee); by Brahman is the oblation poured into the fire of Brahman; Brahman verily shall be reached by him who always sees Brahman in action.

anvaya.base: अर्पण · offering; that by which one offers

anvaya.meaning: into the fire that is Brahman
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्मन् (Brahman) + अग्नि (fire): the fire which is Brahman

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular (offered)
gerundive, neuter, nominative singular (must be reached)

anvaya.meaning: by one absorbed in Brahman as action
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्मन् (Brahman) + कर्मन् (action) + समाधि (absorption): one whose absorption is in action seen as Brahman

verses.explanation: The sacrifice analyzed into its components — instrument, offering, fire, offerer, act, and goal — and each found to be the same one substance. When every coordinate of an action is seen as Brahman, the action stops being a transaction between separate things and becomes the Absolute moving within itself; it has nowhere to land as karma. Brahmārpaṇam brahma haviḥ is the verse chanted before meals across India, turning every table into the altar it describes: the most ordinary act of eating becomes the daily rehearsal of this vision.
verses.connection: Detonates the word yajna from 4.23: sacrifice is no longer a rite within reality — reality itself is the rite.
verses.reflection: Before one meal or task, see Brahman as the offering, the act, the doer — and the day turns altar.
verses.background: Krishna has just said that the works of one who acts for sacrifice melt away entirely. Śaṅkara asks how a deed already under way can vanish without bearing its result; this verse gives the reason in the language of the fire ritual. Brahman is the one reality underlying all things.
verses.hook: How does someone fully absorbed in God see an act of offering?

refs.note: Calls the highest devotee one who sees God in all beings and all beings in God.
Says the soul is God's energy and Krishna is the energetic, so the soul is both one with and different from him.

views.text: Brahma and arpaṇam are not a compound: to the knower, what appears as the ladle is Brahman, as the silver seen in mother-of-pearl is only mother-of-pearl. For him action is sublated and ceases.
Ladle, oblation and fire are called Brahman because they are effects of Brahman, its body. Contemplating Brahman as the soul of every act turns that act into a form of knowledge.
The oblation is the whole visible universe, poured back into the fire of tranquil supreme consciousness from which it came, to increase its light; the act itself becomes contemplation.
Everything, including the soul, is God's energy, one with and distinct from him. Those fully absorbed in God see the offerer, the offering, the fire and the act itself as non-different from him.

verses.devanagari:
दैवमेवापरे यज्ञं योगिनः पर्युपासते ।
ब्रह्माग्नावपरे यज्ञं यज्ञेनैवोपजुह्वति॥
verses.transliteration:
daivamevāpare yajñaṃ yoginaḥ paryupāsate
brahmāgnāvapare yajñaṃ yajñenaivopajuhvati
verses.essence: Some yogis offer sacrifice to the gods; others offer sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman.
verses.translation: Some Yogies perform sacrifice to the gods alone; while others (who have realised the Self) offer the self as sacrifice by the Self in the fire of Brahman alone.

anvaya.base: दैव · relating to the gods (from देव)
anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, accusative singular, agreeing with यज्ञम्
verb, present, middle voice, 3rd person plural

anvaya.meaning: into the fire that is Brahman
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्मन् (Brahman) + अग्नि (fire): the fire which is Brahman

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)

verses.explanation: A catalogue of fires begins (4.25–30), and its first entry sets the range: from the familiar deva-yajña of altar and ghee to the vertiginous act of offering the very sense of separate sacrifice into the One. Every spiritual practice, the list will argue, is some arrangement of offering and fire.
verses.connection: Begins cashing out 4.24: if all is Brahman, then everything humans do toward the sacred is a species of one yajna.
verses.reflection: Whatever your form of sacrifice — service, study, craft — perform it today as sacrifice, knowingly.
verses.background: Having described knowledge as a sacrifice, Krishna begins a list of other sacrifices. Śrīdhara counts eight verses in it, each kind suited to a different type of seeker, all leading up to praise of knowledge above them. This verse gives the first two kinds.
verses.hook: What different kinds of sacrifice do yogis offer?

views.text: In the second line yajña means the Self: offering the Self in the fire of Brahman is realizing that the self, seen with its limiting adjuncts, is the unconditioned Brahman.

Rejects reading the gods as the senses. Ritualists who offer to Indra and others with no craving for fruit, simply because it is to be done, pour that very rite into Brahman, and so they too reach Brahman.
The first group are karma-yogins who worship Indra and the rest without seeing Brahman in them; the second are jñāna-yogins who dissolve every rite in Brahman, and this is the sacrifice of knowledge.

People sacrifice according to their understanding: those wanting material rewards offer to the celestial gods, while those with deeper insight offer their very selves to the Supreme through complete surrender.

verses.devanagari:
श्रोत्रादीनीन्द्रियाण्यन्ये संयमाग्निषु जुह्वति ।
शब्दादीन्विषयानन्य इन्द्रियाग्निषु जुह्वति॥
verses.transliteration:
śrotrādīnīndriyāṇyanye saṃyamāgniṣu juhvati
śabdādīnviṣayānanya indriyāgniṣu juhvati
verses.essence: Some offer hearing and the other senses into the fires of restraint; others offer sound and the other objects into the fires of the senses.
verses.translation: Some again offer the organ of hearing and other senses as sacrifice in the fire of restraint; others offer sound and other objects of the senses as sacrifice in the fire of the senses.

anvaya.base: श्रोत्रादि · the ear and so on
anvaya.parts: श्रोत्र (ear, hearing) + आदि (and so on): those beginning with hearing
संयम (restraint) + अग्नि (fire): fires which are restraint
शब्द (sound) + आदि (and so on): those beginning with sound

anvaya.meaning: into the fires of the senses
anvaya.parts: इन्द्रिय (sense) + अग्नि (fire): fires which are the senses

verses.explanation: Two opposite disciplines, both consecrated: the ascetic pours the senses themselves into restraint's fire — withdrawal as oblation; the householder pours objects into the senses' fire — engagement, but as conscious offering rather than grabbing. The Gita refuses to rank them; what sanctifies is the offering-posture, not the direction of flow.
verses.connection: Extends 4.25 inward: renunciation and right enjoyment are both fires, both valid altars.
verses.reflection: Offer one sense into restraint today, or one object into a sense, deliberately — both are valid fires.
verses.background: The list of sacrifices continues with two more, both concerned with the senses. Śrīdhara assigns them to two ways of life: the lifelong celibate student, who holds the senses back, and the householder, who meets their objects without attachment.
verses.hook: Should you shut the senses down or use them differently?

views.text: 'Fires' is plural because restraint is practised for each sense separately. The second group treat their perception of objects not forbidden by scripture as a sacrifice.
The second offering is enjoyment pursued only to burn away the sense of difference between enjoyer and enjoyed; in true enjoyment the object never stands apart from the one who enjoys it.

The first group are lifelong celibates who dissolve the senses in restraint; the second are householders who stay unattached even while enjoying, treating the senses as fire and their objects as oblation.
One path forcibly withdraws the senses, as in hatha yoga; the other, bhakti, trains them to see God in everything. The devotional way is easier, more joyful and less prone to falls.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वाणीन्द्रियकर्माणि प्राणकर्माणि चापरे ।
आत्मसंयमयोगाग्नौ जुह्वति ज्ञानदीपिते॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvāṇīndriyakarmāṇi prāṇakarmāṇi cāpare
ātmasaṃyamayogāgnau juhvati jñānadīpite
verses.essence: Others offer all the workings of the senses and of the life-breath into the fire of self-restraint kindled by knowledge.
verses.translation: Others again sacrifice all the functions of the senses and those of the breath (vital energy or Prana) in the fire of the Yoga of self-restraint kindled by knowledge.

anvaya.form: noun compound, neuter, accusative plural (the object)
anvaya.parts: इन्द्रिय (sense) + कर्मन् (action): the actions of the senses

anvaya.form: noun compound, neuter, accusative plural (the object)
anvaya.parts: प्राण (vital breath) + कर्मन् (action): the functions of the vital breath

anvaya.meaning: into the fire of self-restraint yoga
anvaya.base: आत्मसंयमयोगाग्नि · fire of the yoga of self-control
anvaya.parts: आत्मन् (self) + संयम (restraint) + योग (yoga) + अग्नि (fire): the fire that is the yoga of self-restraint

anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, locative singular, agreeing with the fire
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + दीपित (lit, kindled): set alight by knowledge

verses.explanation: The totalizing version: not this sense or that object, but the entire traffic of perception and vitality, fed into one inward fire — and the kindling is named: jñāna-dīpite, lit by knowledge. Discipline without understanding is cold ash; understanding makes restraint combust into transformation.
verses.connection: Deepens 4.26: from selective offerings to the whole apparatus, with knowledge as the match.
verses.reflection: Pour a scattered hour into one-pointed attention and call it by its true name: oblation.
verses.background: A fifth kind of sacrifice follows the four of 4.25–26. Śrīdhara assigns it to those devoted to meditation, as distinct from the celibate students and householders of the previous verse.
verses.hook: How do some seekers use knowledge to restrain the senses and breath?

refs.note: The teaching 'you are That', one of the aphorisms jñāna yogis contemplate while withdrawing the senses into self-knowledge.
The statement 'I am Brahman', another aphorism used as an aid to the contemplation this verse describes.
Says the path of knowledge suits only those already deeply detached, showing how hard this discipline is.

views.text: Ātma-saṃyama is withdrawal into the Self, and that is the fire of yoga; discriminating knowledge makes it blaze, as oil makes a lamp blaze.
By contemplating the self, the practitioner keeps the mind from clinging to the work of senses and breath, and overcomes even subtle lingering desires for them.

These are the meditators. The functions of the senses of knowing and of action, and of all ten breaths, five main and five minor, are offered into one-pointed meditation lit by clear knowledge of its object.

Jñāna yogis withdraw the senses not by brute will but by constant discrimination, contemplating the self as distinct from body and mind. It is a demanding path needing a trained intellect and strong renunciation.

verses.devanagari:
द्रव्ययज्ञास्तपोयज्ञा योगयज्ञास्तथापरे ।
स्वाध्यायज्ञानयज्ञाश्च यतयः संशितव्रताः॥
verses.transliteration:
dravyayajñāstapoyajñā yogayajñāstathāpare
svādhyāyajñānayajñāśca yatayaḥ saṃśitavratāḥ
verses.essence: Others offer wealth, austerity and yoga as sacrifice; ascetics of sharp vows offer study and knowledge.
verses.translation: Others again offer wealth, austerity and Yoga as sacrifice, while the ascetics of self-restraint and rigid vows offer study of scriptures and knowledge as sacrifice.

anvaya.parts: द्रव्य (material wealth) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): those whose sacrifice is material goods
तपस् (austerity) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): those whose sacrifice is austerity
योग (yoga) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): those whose sacrifice is yoga practice

anvaya.meaning: whose sacrifice is study and knowledge
anvaya.base: स्वाध्यायज्ञानयज्ञ · sacrificer of study and knowledge
anvaya.parts: स्वाध्याय (scriptural study) + ज्ञान (knowledge) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): those whose sacrifice is study and understanding
संशित (sharpened, strict) + व्रत (vow): those whose vows are rigorous

verses.explanation: The list widens to cover whole lifestyles: the philanthropist's giving, the ascetic's heat, the yogi's practice, the scholar's svādhyāya — each a complete religious path when performed as offering. The altar is no longer confined to the ritual ground: anything poured out with the right inner posture becomes sacred fire.
verses.connection: Continues 4.25–27's democratization of yajna into the great human vocations.
verses.reflection: Choose your altar today — possessions, austerity, practice, or study — and place something real on it.
verses.background: Krishna is still listing for Arjuna the many forms sacrifice takes among different seekers. After the inner offerings of senses and mind in 4.26–27, this verse adds the outward ones: giving away wealth, austerities such as fasting, yogic absorption, and the study and understanding of scripture by ascetics of strict vows.
verses.hook: What else can people offer as sacrifice besides ritual offerings?

refs.note: Patañjali says perfection in samādhi comes from surrender to God, so even yogic practice must be offered in devotion.
True knowledge is that which increases devotion to God, the spirit in which study becomes sacrifice.

views.text: Counts six kinds of sacrifice. Svādhyāya is recitation of the Veda according to rule; the sacrifice of knowledge is grasping the meaning of scripture.
Since the context is karma-yoga, yoga-yajña here means pilgrimage to holy places. All these sacrificers share self-control and firm vows.
Yoga here is samādhi, the stilling of the mind's movements; austerity means disciplines like the kṛcchra and cāndrāyaṇa fasts; and study and knowledge may be one sacrifice or two.
Sacrifice takes many forms suited to different natures: wealth given to a divine cause, yogic practice, or scriptural study. Each purifies when dedicated to God.

verses.devanagari:
अपाने जुह्वति प्राणं प्राणेऽपानं तथापरे ।
प्राणापानगती रुद्ध्वा प्राणायामपरायणाः॥
verses.transliteration:
apāne juhvati prāṇaṃ prāṇe'pānaṃ tathāpare
prāṇāpānagatī ruddhvā prāṇāyāmaparāyaṇāḥ
verses.essence: Others offer the inbreath into the outbreath and the outbreath into the inbreath, restraining both — intent on pranayama.
verses.translation: Others offer as sacrifice the outgoing breath in the incoming, and the incoming in the outgoing, restraining the course of the outgoing and the incoming breaths, solely absorbed in the restraint of the breath.

anvaya.base: प्राण · life-breath; here the outgoing current
प्राण · life-breath; here the outgoing current
प्राणापानगति · movement of prāṇa and apāna
anvaya.form: noun compound, feminine, accusative dual (both courses)
anvaya.parts: प्राण (out-breath) + अपान (in-breath) + गति (movement): the two movements of the breaths
प्राणायाम (breath control) + परायण (wholly intent on): those for whom breath-control is the chief aim

verses.explanation: Breath itself becomes the altar: outflow offered into inflow, inflow into outflow, and in the third practice both held — the moment of stillness between breaths treated as the sanctum. The body's most automatic act, made deliberate, becomes liturgy. Pranayama enters the Gita not as exercise but as sacrifice.
verses.connection: The subtlest fire yet in the catalogue: the offering and the fire are both made of breath.
verses.reflection: Watch your breath for ten cycles, in and out as mutual offerings, and find the oldest ritual.
verses.background: The list of sacrifices continues. Having named offerings of wealth, austerity and study, Krishna turns to those devoted to breath control, describing how they offer the incoming and outgoing breaths into each other and then hold both still.
verses.hook: How do some seekers make their breathing an offering?

views.text: Maps the verse onto three breath practices: filling in (pūraka), emptying out (recaka) and holding (kumbhaka), the holding done constantly after the other two.
Reads 4.29 and 4.30 together: the 'regulated food' of the next verse applies to all three kinds of breath-practitioner, not to a fourth group.
When the breath is mastered the mind stops wandering and the senses grow quiet, because the activity of mind and senses runs on the vibration of prāṇa.

Breath-control practices help tame the senses and focus the mind, which is then offered to God. Done as sacrifice to the Supreme, such austerities purify the heart; advanced breath retention needs a qualified teacher.

verses.devanagari:
अपरे नियताहाराः प्राणान्प्राणेषु जुह्वति ।
सर्वेऽप्येते यज्ञविदो यज्ञक्षपितकल्मषाः॥
verses.transliteration:
apare niyatāhārāḥ prāṇānprāṇeṣu juhvati
sarve'pyete yajñavido yajñakṣapitakalmaṣāḥ
verses.essence: Others, of regulated food, offer the breaths into the breaths. All these are knowers of sacrifice, their stains destroyed by sacrifice.
verses.translation: Others who regulate their diet offer life-breaths in life-breaths. All these are knowers of sacrifice, whose sins are destroyed by sacrifice.

anvaya.parts: नियत (regulated) + आहार (food): those whose food is restricted
यज्ञ (sacrifice) + विद् (knower): those who understand sacrifice
यज्ञ (sacrifice) + क्षपित (destroyed) + कल्मष (impurity, sin): those whose impurities sacrifice has destroyed

verses.explanation: The catalogue closes with one more entry — those who regulate their food and offer breath into breath — and then the great equalizing verdict: sarve 'pi ete, *all* of these, from the ghee-pourer to the breath-watcher, are yajña-vids whose stains the practice burns. Every fire on the list truly purifies; the one ranking waits for 4.33, where the sacrifice of knowledge is set above the sacrifice of material things.
verses.connection: Concludes the survey of 4.25–30 and certifies every entry: the form varies, the purification does not.
verses.reflection: Even your disciplined eating is a sacrifice; treat one meal today with a priest's attention.
verses.background: Krishna adds the last entry to his list, those who restrict their food, and then sums up the whole series from 4.25: every one of these seekers, whatever the form of their offering, knows what sacrifice is and is cleansed by it.
verses.hook: What do all these different sacrifices have in common?

views.text: Whichever function of the breath is brought under control, the other functions are offered into it and merge there, as it were.
Their sins are removed because these practices rest on the daily and occasional rites, preceded by the five great sacrifices of 3.10; living on sacrificial remains, they go to Brahman.

Regulated food means shrinking one's intake until the senses' functions fade of themselves. An alternative reading of the breath verses: each in-breath and out-breath carries the unspoken mantra haṃsaḥ–so'ham, a meditation on the unity of 'that' and 'thou'.

Fasting and regulating diet are also sacrifices, weakening the senses' pull toward pleasure. All such austerities aim to curb the urge for sense gratification, and offered to God they purify the heart.

verses.devanagari:
यज्ञशिष्टामृतभुजो यान्ति ब्रह्म सनातनम् ।
नायं लोकोऽस्त्ययज्ञस्य कुतोऽन्यः कुरुसत्तम॥
verses.transliteration:
yajñaśiṣṭāmṛtabhujo yānti brahma sanātanam
nāyaṃ loko'styayajñasya kuto'nyaḥ kurusattama
verses.essence: Eaters of the nectar of sacrifice's remnant go to the eternal Brahman. Not even this world is for the non-sacrificer — how then the other, Kurusattama?
verses.translation: Those who eat the remnants of the sacrifice, which are like nectar, go to the eternal Brahman. This world is not for the man who does not perform sacrifice; how then can he have the other, O Arjuna?

anvaya.meaning: eaters of the nectar left from sacrifice
