anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, nominative plural (the subject)
anvaya.parts: यज्ञ (sacrifice) + शिष्ट (remnant) + अमृत (nectar) + भुज् (eater): those who eat the nectar that remains after sacrifice

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, accusative singular, agreeing with ब्रह्म

anvaya.meaning: for one who offers no sacrifice
anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, genitive singular (for him)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): one without sacrifice

anvaya.form: pronominal adjective, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)

anvaya.parts: कुरु (the Kuru clan) + सत्तम (best): best among the Kurus

verses.explanation: Chapter 3's leftover-eaters (3.13) return transfigured: the remnant of any true offering is now amṛta, nectar, and its eaters travel to Brahman itself. The closing logic cuts hard: the non-offerer fails even here — a life of pure taking cannot build a livable world, let alone a higher one. Sacrifice is not piety added to life; it is life's load-bearing wall.
verses.connection: Caps the catalogue with destination and warning, echoing 3.12–13 at a higher octave.
verses.reflection: Taste the remnant of sacrifice — the peace after selfless work — and let it spoil cheaper sweets.
verses.background: With the list of sacrifices complete, Krishna tells Arjuna what they lead to and what is lost without them. Śrīdhara reads the second half as the fault of not sacrificing, so that sacrifice must be done in every way: even this world is closed to the one who never offers.
verses.hook: What do you gain from what remains after a sacrifice?

refs.note: Uddhava vows to use only what has first been offered to Krishna, saying those who live on his remnants conquer illusion.

views.text: If such sacrificers seek liberation, they reach Brahman in due course, by stages, not at once. Without even one of these sacrifices, even this common world is lost, let alone a higher one.
'This world' stands for the worldly aims of virtue, wealth and pleasure; one who skips the daily sacrifices cannot gain even these, so how could he gain release, the highest aim?
The nectar is the bliss of resting in one's own Self that remains once the senses' deities are satisfied. Such people, remaining Brahman, move freely in ordinary life.
What remains after offering something to God becomes his grace, and partaking of it purifies and uplifts. Those who make no such offering stay entangled in the reactions of their work.

verses.devanagari:
एवं बहुविधा यज्ञा वितता ब्रह्मणो मुखे ।
कर्मजान्विद्धि तान्सर्वानेवं ज्ञात्वा विमोक्ष्यसे॥
verses.transliteration:
evaṃ bahuvidhā yajñā vitatā brahmaṇo mukhe
karmajānviddhi tānsarvānevaṃ jñātvā vimokṣyase
verses.essence: Thus many kinds of sacrifice are spread in the mouth of Brahman. Know them all as born of action; knowing thus, you shall be freed.
verses.translation: Thus, manifold sacrifices are spread out before Brahman (literally) at the mouth or face of Brahman). Know them all as born of action and thus knowing, thou shalt be liberated.

anvaya.parts: बहु (many) + विधा (kind): of many kinds

anvaya.meaning: in the mouth, at the door

anvaya.parts: कर्मन् (action) + ज (born): born of action

anvaya.form: verb, future, middle voice, 2nd person singular (you will be freed)

verses.explanation: Two liberating observations: the many fires all open into one mouth — diversity of practice, single destination; and karma-jān, every one of them is made of *action*, of body, speech and breath actually doing something. No sacrifice on the list is performed by the Self, which only watches. See that, and the doer-knot loosens for good.
verses.connection: Distills 4.25–31: all the fires are one fire, and all of them burn on the far side of the witnessing Self.
verses.reflection: Many fires, one altar: stop ranking your neighbor's discipline against yours today.
verses.background: Krishna gathers up the many sacrifices he has just described. Śrīdhara says he concludes them here in order to go on and praise the sacrifice of knowledge: all these are enjoined by the Veda, yet all arise from action of speech, mind and body, which never touches the Self.
verses.hook: Why does the Veda describe so many different sacrifices?

views.text: 'In the mouth of Brahman' means taught through the Vedas. These sacrifices are works of body, speech and mind, not of the actionless Self; knowing 'these are not my actions' is what frees.
The sacrifices are spread out as means to Brahman, that is, to realizing the self's true nature. 'Born of action' means they grow out of the daily and occasional rites.
The Vedas offer many sacrifices to suit different natures, but the common thread is doing them with devotion for God. Knowing this, one is not confused by varied instructions and can be freed.

verses.devanagari:
श्रेयान्द्रव्यमयाद्यज्ञाज्ज्ञानयज्ञः परन्तप ।
सर्वं कर्माखिलं पार्थ ज्ञाने परिसमाप्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
śreyāndravyamayādyajñājjñānayajñaḥ parantapa
sarvaṃ karmākhilaṃ pārtha jñāne parisamāpyate
verses.essence: Better than the sacrifice of things is the sacrifice of knowledge, Parantapa; all action without remainder, Partha, culminates in knowledge.
verses.translation: Superior is wisdom-sacrifice to the sacrifice with objects, O Parantapa (scorcher of the foes). All actions in their entirety, O Arjuna, culminate in knowledge.

anvaya.form: adjective, comparative, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
adjective with suffix -मय (made of), masculine, ablative singular (than)
noun compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): the sacrifice that is knowledge
पर (enemy) + तप (one who scorches): one who burns his enemies

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, nominative singular, agreeing with कर्म

anvaya.base: परि-सम्-√आप् · to be completed, end in
anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is brought to completion)

verses.explanation: After honoring every fire equally, one ranking after all: jñāna-yajña stands above the offerings of stuff — not because things are base, but because all action, traced to its end, parisamāpyate, terminates in knowing. Works are the river; knowledge is the sea they were always running toward. The chapter now turns to how such knowledge is obtained.
verses.connection: The hinge from the yajna-catalogue to the knowledge-finale (4.34–42): every fire was kindling for this one.
verses.reflection: Prefer the knowledge-offering today: understand one thing deeply rather than performing three things outwardly.
verses.background: Having summed up the varied sacrifices, Krishna now ranks them for Arjuna. Śaṅkara notes that the teaching began with complete knowledge pictured as a sacrifice in 4.24; here that knowledge-sacrifice is set against all the offerings made with material things.
verses.text_note: The translation of this verse was missing in the source dataset; it is taken from the Sivananda text in the gita/gita dataset.
verses.hook: Is sacrifice done with knowledge better than offering material things?

views.text: Knowledge-sacrifice also involves the mind, but knowledge, being the Self, is only revealed in a state of mind, never produced by it. That is why it surpasses offerings made of things.

Material sacrifices bring material results and lead back to this world for enjoyment; the sacrifice of wisdom leads to liberation. As rivers join the ocean, all actions, by purifying the heart, end in knowledge.

Rituals, fasts and chants done mechanically are better than nothing but cannot purify the mind; the mind must be engaged. Knowing God and our relationship with him nourishes devotion, so sacrifice in knowledge is superior.

verses.devanagari:
तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया ।
उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः॥
verses.transliteration:
tadviddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā
upadekṣyanti te jñānaṃ jñāninastattvadarśinaḥ
verses.essence: Learn that by prostration, by inquiry, by service; the knowers, the seers of truth, will teach you knowledge.
verses.translation: Know That by long prostration, by question and by service; the wise who have realised the Truth will instruct thee in (that) knowledge.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
noun, feminine, instrumental singular (by means of)

anvaya.parts: तत्त्व (truth, reality) + दर्शिन् (seer): those who have seen the truth

verses.explanation: How the highest yajña is lit: not from books alone but from those already lit. Three approaches form the protocol — praṇipāta, the bow that lowers the vessel below the source; paripraśna, questioning about bondage and freedom that is persistent yet sincere (not the cavilling of 3.32); sevā, service that proves the asking is serious. This is not blind reception but engaged humility. And the teacher must be doubly qualified: jñānin *and* tattva-darśin — learned, and having seen. Transmission, here, is from sight to sight.
verses.connection: Answers the question 4.33 raises: where does knowledge-sacrifice get its flame? From those already burning.
verses.reflection: Approach someone who knows, with a real question, real respect, and real willingness to serve.
verses.background: Krishna has just said that all action ends in knowledge. Śrīdhara introduces this verse as the means to that knowledge of the Self: Arjuna is told how to approach those who have seen the truth so that they will teach it to him.
verses.hook: How do you actually gain spiritual knowledge?

refs.note: Says one who has a teacher comes to know, supporting the need to approach a realised Guru.
Teaches that an intellect clouded by ignorance cannot free itself; knowledge must come from one who knows the truth.
Prahlāda says the mind cannot touch God's feet until one is bathed in the dust of a saint's feet.

views.text: Asks about bondage and liberation, knowledge and ignorance. 'Who have seen the Truth' is added because only knowledge taught by the fully enlightened becomes effective; learning alone is not enough.
The knowledge is the teaching on the self given in 2.17–39. The wise, honoured by prostration and seeing your desire to know in your questions, will teach it to you.
Prostration is devotion, inquiry is careful reasoning, service is practice. The 'knowers' who show the truth can be one's own senses, lit by consciousness; read conventionally, it means other sages.

The Absolute cannot be grasped by our own thinking. One must approach a God-realised Guru, inquire humbly and serve him; spiritual knowledge is revealed by the Guru's grace to a humble, serving disciple.

verses.devanagari:
यज्ज्ञात्वा न पुनर्मोहमेवं यास्यसि पाण्डव ।
येन भूतान्यशेषेण द्रक्ष्यस्यात्मन्यथो मयि॥
verses.transliteration:
yajjñātvā na punarmohamevaṃ yāsyasi pāṇḍava
yena bhūtānyaśeṣeṇa drakṣyasyātmanyatho mayi
verses.essence: Knowing which, you will not fall into delusion again, Pandava — by it you will see all beings in the Self, and then in me.
verses.translation: Knowing that thou shalt not, O Arjuna, again get deluded like this; and by that thou shalt see all beings in thy Self and also in Me.

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, neuter, instrumental singular (by which)

anvaya.parts: अ (no) + शेष (remainder): leaving nothing out

verses.explanation: What the teachers of 4.34 transmit, in two movements: first, all beings seen within the one Self — separateness healed; then, that Self seen within Krishna — the many found in oneself, and oneself found in the Lord. And the practical guarantee Arjuna most needs: na punar moham, no relapse. The confusion of chapter 1 is not to be managed but ended.
verses.connection: States the content and the cure: this knowledge answers 1.28–47 at the root, permanently.
verses.reflection: Imagine seeing all beings in yourself for one minute — and let delusion lose its favorite argument.
verses.background: Krishna now tells Arjuna what the knowledge taught by the seers will do for him. Śrīdhara says this verse and the next two and a half give its fruit, beginning with the delusion Arjuna fell into on the battlefield over killing his own kinsmen.
verses.hook: What changes in how you see others once you gain this knowledge?

refs.note: Hanumān says he sees Sītā and Rāma in all the world and so bows to everyone, the vision this verse describes.

views.text: Seeing all beings, from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, in the Self and in Me means realizing the identity of the individual Self and the Lord taught in the Upanishads.
You see beings in yourself because every self, freed from matter, has the same nature of knowledge; you see them in Me by their likeness to the Lord's nature, not by sharing his powers.

The delusion ended is the one about killing kinsmen. Father, son and the rest, shaped by one's own ignorance, are seen as not different from the Self, and then that Self as not different from the Supreme.
Once enlightened, the soul is never again overcome by illusion. It sees the world as God's energy and all beings as his parts, holding a divine attitude toward everyone.

verses.devanagari:
अपि चेदसि पापेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः पापकृत्तमः ।
सर्वं ज्ञानप्लवेनैव वृजिनं सन्तरिष्यसि॥
verses.transliteration:
api cedasi pāpebhyaḥ sarvebhyaḥ pāpakṛttamaḥ
sarvaṃ jñānaplavenaiva vṛjinaṃ santariṣyasi
verses.essence: Even if you were the most sinful of all sinners, by the raft of knowledge alone you would cross over all wickedness.
verses.translation: Even if thou art the most sinful of all sinners, yet thou shalt verily cross all sins by the raft of knowledge.

anvaya.form: adjective used as a noun, masculine, ablative plural (than: comparison)
adjective, superlative (suffix -तम, most), masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: पाप (sin) + कृत् (doer): doer of sin, with -तम: the worst

anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + प्लव (raft, boat): the raft which is knowledge

verses.explanation: The amnesty clause, stated at the limit case: take the worst record imaginable — knowledge still carries it across. The image is exact: a raft does not dry up the river of past karma; it keeps the passenger above it during the crossing. Sin, in this vision, is not a stain requiring eternal payment but a weight requiring sufficient buoyancy.
verses.connection: Pre-empts Arjuna's lingering terror from 1.36–45: no accumulated guilt disqualifies the knower.
verses.reflection: Whatever your worst chapter, the raft of knowing still floats — step on, today, from where you are.
verses.background: Continuing the praise of knowledge, Krishna speaks to the fear of sin that has weighed on Arjuna since he first refused to fight his kinsmen. Śaṅkara leads in by saying the greatness of knowledge is now being told.
verses.hook: Can even the worst sinner cross beyond their sins?

refs.note: Says one whose intellect is the driver and who holds the mind's reins reaches the end of the road, Viṣṇu's supreme abode.

views.text: For one seeking liberation, even formal righteousness counts as a fault to be crossed; the whole ocean of it is crossed by knowledge alone, used as a float.
Stresses the ease of it: on the ship of knowledge even the greatest sinner crosses the whole sea of sin well and without strain.
Material existence is an ocean of suffering, and divine knowledge is the boat across it. Acts that bind the ignorant liberate the knowing when done as offerings to God.

yathaidhāṃsi samiddho'gnirbhasmasātkurute'rjuna
jñānāgniḥ sarvakarmāṇi bhasmasātkurute tathā
verses.essence: As a kindled fire reduces firewood to ash, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all karma to ash.
verses.translation: As the blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes.

noun compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)

verses.explanation: The raft becomes a furnace. Logs do not negotiate with fire, do not get partially excused — they become ash, a substance that can never be wood again. So with karma met by realized knowledge: not suspended, not forgiven on probation, but converted past recall. Bhasmasāt — 'wholly into ash' — names a change that cannot be undone. Only the karma already running this body's life is left to play out.
verses.connection: Intensifies 4.36: crossing over becomes burning up — the residue itself is destroyed.
verses.reflection: Feed one old karma to the fire of understanding today: see it fully, and watch it turn to ash.
verses.background: Krishna has called knowledge a raft that carries one across the sea of sin. Śrīdhara says this verse removes a mistaken idea that crossing over merely leaves the sin in place, like an ocean behind a ship; an image from fire shows that the sin itself is destroyed.
verses.hook: What can burn away the karma of countless past lives?

views.text: Knowledge does not burn actions directly like wood; by ending ignorance it makes them powerless. The karma that already produced this body is used up only by living it out.
The practical point: keep the fire of knowledge well fed with the firm conviction that comes from steady practice.
The verse answers a doubt left by 4.36: a raft only crosses a sea that remains. Fire actually destroys, so knowledge burns all karma except what has already begun to bear fruit.
Exhausting our vast store of karma by experiencing its results would take endless lifetimes. Knowledge of the soul and God leads to surrender, and God then burns that stockpile in this very life.

verses.devanagari:
न हि ज्ञानेन सदृशं पवित्रमिह विद्यते ।
तत्स्वयं योगसंसिद्धः कालेनात्मनि विन्दति॥
verses.transliteration:
na hi jñānena sadṛśaṃ pavitramiha vidyate
tatsvayaṃ yogasaṃsiddhaḥ kālenātmani vindati
verses.essence: Nothing here purifies like knowledge. One perfected in yoga finds it, in time, within oneself.
verses.translation: Verily, there is no purifier in this world like knowledge. He who is perfected in Yoga finds it in the Self in time.

verb, present, middle voice, 3rd person singular
adjective compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + संसिद्ध (perfected): one perfected by yoga

verses.explanation: The superlative and the timetable. No purifier matches knowledge — not pilgrimage, fire, or austerity, each of which cleans a layer while knowledge dissolves the misidentification beneath all layers. And the finding is svayam… ātmani: by oneself, within oneself, once one is yoga-saṃsiddha, made ready by practice, and kālena, in time. The practice ripens the vessel; the knowing then arrives like a season, not a seizure. The teacher of 4.34 points; the treasure was always under the student's own floor.
verses.connection: Crowns the fire-and-raft verses and relocates the prize: knowledge is found, not imported.
verses.reflection: Trust the timeline: purified by practice, clarity finds you by itself, in time, within.
verses.background: After the raft and the fire, Krishna gives the reason knowledge has such power. Śrīdhara adds the implied question: if knowledge purifies like nothing else, why does not everyone simply practise it? The second half answers that it comes in time to one made fit by the yoga of action.
verses.hook: What purifies you more than anything else in this world?

refs.note: Patañjali says knowledge realised within through yoga differs from and surpasses knowledge from scripture and inference.

views.text: Yoga-saṃsiddhaḥ is the seeker made fit through karma-yoga and the yoga of concentration; after a long time he finds knowledge by himself, in his own heart.
Other things purify only through the touch of consciousness, not by their own nature; knowledge alone is pure in itself, as the fully enlightened discover for themselves.
Answers why everyone does not simply practise self-knowledge: it comes of itself only to one made fit by long karma-yoga, not without it.
Knowledge purifies like nothing else, but theory alone is like memorising a cookbook without cooking. Only practice that purifies the mind brings inner realisation, the purest knowledge.

verses.devanagari:

verses.transliteration:
śraddhāvāṃllabhate jñānaṃ tatparaḥ saṃyatendriyaḥ
jñānaṃ labdhvā parāṃ śāntimacireṇādhigacchati
verses.essence: The one of faith, devoted to it, senses mastered, attains knowledge; having attained knowledge, one quickly reaches the supreme peace.
verses.translation: The man who is full of faith, who is devoted to it, and who has subdued the senses obtains (this) knowledge; and having obtained the knowledge he attains at once to the supreme peace.

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, accusative singular, agreeing with शान्तिम्

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + चिर (long time): without delay

verses.explanation: The recipe in three ingredients: śraddhā, not credulity but working trust, the confidence that lets practice run long enough to verify; tatparatā, making it the chief pursuit rather than a hobby; saṁyatendriyatā, senses gathered so the inquiry has fuel. Then the timeline shifts: acireṇa, *without delay* — knowledge, and then the supreme peace. The path is long only while one walks it half-turned-around.
verses.connection: Names who actually finds what 4.38 promised — and the speed available to the wholehearted.
verses.reflection: Bring faith, devotion, and governed senses to your study today — the three keys that open texts.
verses.background: Krishna has said that knowledge comes in time to one perfected in yoga. Śaṅkara leads in by naming the sure means by which it is gained. Here Krishna says who receives it and what follows once it is won.
verses.hook: What do you need in order to gain this knowledge?

refs.note: Says the truths of scripture reveal themselves to one with supreme devotion to God and equal devotion to the Guru.

views.text: Each qualifier closes a gap: the faithful may be lazy, hence 'devoted'; the devoted may lack control, hence 'senses restrained'. Prostration can be faked, but these three never fail to bring knowledge.
Faith here is firm trust that the knowledge received by instruction will ripen; the supreme peace is nirvāṇa, the realization of the self.
Faith means confidence in what the teacher taught. Before knowledge, karma-yoga is still to be practised for purity; once knowledge is gained nothing remains to be done.
Some truths can only be experienced after progress, so faith lets us accept what we cannot yet grasp. It must not be blind: first verify that a Guru is genuine, then deepen faith and surrender.

अज्ञश्चाश्रद्दधानश्च संशयात्मा विनश्यति ।
नायं लोकोऽस्ति न परो न सुखं संशयात्मनः॥
verses.transliteration:
ajñaścāśraddadhānaśca saṃśayātmā vinaśyati
nāyaṃ loko'sti na paro na sukhaṃ saṃśayātmanaḥ
verses.essence: The ignorant, the faithless and the doubting self perish. For the doubter there is neither this world nor the next, nor happiness.
verses.translation: The ignorant the faithless, the doubting self goes to destruction; there is neither this world nor the other, nor happiness for the doubting.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + ज्ञ (knowing): one who does not know

anvaya.form: present participle with negative अ, masculine, nominative singular (the subject) (one without faith)
noun compound, masculine, nominative singular (the subject)
anvaya.parts: संशय (doubt) + आत्मन् (self, mind): one whose mind is made of doubt

anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, genitive singular (for him)
anvaya.parts: संशय (doubt) + आत्मन् (self): the doubting one

verses.explanation: Three failure modes, and the verse reserves its full sentence for the third: not honest ignorance, not even unbelief, but saṁśayātmā — the one whose very self has become doubt, the chronic suspender who can neither commit to the world nor to the path. Such a one loses both shores at once. Inquiry is sacred (4.34 commanded it); indefinite hovering is its parasite.
verses.connection: The shadow of 4.39's śraddhā: trust finds quickly; institutionalized doubt finds nothing anywhere.
verses.reflection: Notice doubt's cost honestly: neither this world enjoyed nor the next pursued. Choose a foothold.
verses.background: Having named who is fit for knowledge, Krishna now describes, as Śrīdhara says, its opposite: the one who is unfit. Śaṅkara links the verses directly; liberation follows knowledge, so one must not doubt this, for doubt is the worst of evils.
verses.hook: What happens to someone who lives full of doubt?

refs.note: Ranks aspirants by scriptural knowledge and firm faith; the lowest has weak faith, matching the doubter this verse describes.

views.text: The ignorant and the faithless are ruined, but less than the doubter, who is the worst of all; he can doubt even this world and the next.
Every human aim pursued through scripture needs the firm conviction that the self is other than the body; doubting the self therefore blocks even a little happiness.
The doubter loses this world because he cannot settle on earning or marrying, the next because his dharma never gets done, and happiness because doubt spoils even enjoyment.
Seekers rank by faith and knowledge, and those with neither cannot find peace here or hereafter. Even everyday life runs on trust; one who doubts everything can enjoy nothing.

verses.devanagari:
योगसंन्यस्तकर्माणं ज्ञानसञ्छिन्नसंशयम् ।
आत्मवन्तं न कर्माणि निबध्नन्ति धनञ्जय॥
verses.transliteration:
yogasaṃnyastakarmāṇaṃ jñānasañchinnasaṃśayam
ātmavantaṃ na karmāṇi nibadhnanti dhanañjaya
verses.essence: One whose actions are renounced in yoga, whose doubt is severed by knowledge, who is self-possessed — actions do not bind that one, Dhananjaya.
verses.translation: He who has renounced actions by Yoga, whose doubts are rent asunder by knowledge, and who is self-possessed actions do not bind him, O Arjuna.

anvaya.meaning: who has laid down actions through yoga
anvaya.base: योगसंन्यस्तकर्मन् · renouncer of works by yoga
anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, accusative singular (the object)
anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + संन्यस्त (laid down, renounced) + कर्मन् (action): one who has given up actions through yoga

anvaya.form: adjective compound, masculine, accusative singular (the object)
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + सञ्छिन्न (cut through) + संशय (doubt): one whose doubt is cut away by knowledge
धन (wealth) + जय (winning): winner of wealth

verses.explanation: The chapter gathered into one figure: works laid down *through* yoga (not abandoned but offered — the whole point of 4.20–24), doubt not argued away but *cut* by direct knowledge, and ātmavantam, standing in oneself. Against such a person, karma has lost every handle it ever held.
verses.connection: Synthesis of the chapter's three currents — yajna, jnana, and the severing of 4.40's doubt — in a single freed worker.
verses.reflection: Renounce one fruit consciously, slice one doubt with knowledge, and feel how lightly the day binds.
verses.background: Krishna has just warned that the doubter loses everything. Śrīdhara introduces this verse and the next as the close of the teaching of two chapters, drawing together the way of action and the way of knowledge as two stages of one life rooted in the absolute.
verses.hook: When do actions stop binding a person?

views.text: The yoga through which actions are renounced is knowledge of the supreme goal; ātmavantam means vigilant, never careless. To him actions are only the play of the guṇas.
This verse and the next sum up two chapters' twofold path: actions surrendered to the Lord through worship, and doubt about the body-as-self cut away by knowing the Self as non-doer.
Those who dedicate body, mind and soul to God and act only as service are not bound, because only self-interested action binds. Work offered to God is like multiplying by zero.

verses.devanagari:
तस्मादज्ञानसम्भूतं हृत्स्थं ज्ञानासिनात्मनः ।
छित्त्वैनं संशयं योगमातिष्ठोत्तिष्ठ भारत॥
verses.transliteration:
tasmādajñānasambhūtaṃ hṛtsthaṃ jñānāsinātmanaḥ
chittvainaṃ saṃśayaṃ yogamātiṣṭhottiṣṭha bhārata
verses.essence: Therefore, with the sword of knowledge cut this doubt born of ignorance lodged in your heart. Take refuge in yoga — and stand up, Bharata!
verses.translation: Therefore with the sword of the knowledge (of the Self) cut asunder the doubt of the self born of ignorance, residing in thy heart, and take refuge in Yoga. Arise, O Arjuna.

anvaya.parts: अज्ञान (ignorance) + सम्भूत (born, arisen): born of ignorance
हृद् (heart) + स्थ (standing in): seated in the heart
ज्ञान (knowledge) + असि (sword): the sword which is knowledge

verses.explanation: The chapter ends with steel: jñānāsi, knowledge as sword — fitting tribute to a warrior who will not be healed by anything he cannot wield. The doubt to be cut is hṛt-stham, lodged in the heart, at the seat of understanding itself; arguments alone never reach it. Two final imperatives ring like commands on a field: ātiṣṭha, take your stand; uttiṣṭha, rise. The same word that failed in 2.3 returns — but now the man being raised has been given everything he needs to stand.
verses.connection: Closes the chapter by arming Arjuna against 4.40's enemy — and repeating, with new foundations, the call he once refused.
verses.reflection: Take the sword to your oldest hesitation now — then stand up into the duty it was blocking.
verses.background: This is the last verse of chapter 4. Krishna turns from the teaching back to Arjuna's own situation: the doubt born of grief over killing his kinsmen is still in his heart, and the battle he refused at the start still waits for him.
verses.hook: What should Arjuna do with the doubt lodged in his heart?

views.text: The doubt is called 'your own' because no one can remove another's doubt. Yoga here is doing one's work as a means to illumination, and 'rise' means rise for battle.
Yoga is skill in action; standing up means carrying out one's activities simply because they are to be done.
The heart here means the subtle mind. Having taught karma yoga, Krishna tells Arjuna to cut his doubts with wisdom and faith and rise to do his duty as an offering to God.
